phonemes.desc: Initial character of the restored form Psychḗ.
Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Greek tradition.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PSYCHE' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

kin.label: Greek verb ψύχω
kin.form: psȳkhō, 'to breathe, to blow' — the root of the name; the soul as the body's cool breath. Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek, s.v. ψυχή.

kin.label: Latin form
kin.form: Psychē — the borrowed form Apuleius uses in the Metamorphoses; the romance is traditionally titled 'Cupid and Psyche'.

kin.label: English descendants
kin.form: psyche, psychic, psychology, psychiatry — learned borrowings from Greek that made her name the ordinary word for mind.

pronunciation.note: Psychḗ is Tier 1: Greek ψυχή preserves both the stress (final acute) and the long vowel (η), features the ASCII form psyche flattens. In Homer the word is the life-breath that leaves at death; only later does it become the immortal soul.

domains.title: Soul
domains.subtitle: Soul, Breath, Life
domains.lead: Psychḗ is the Greek word for soul made flesh as a heroine: the life-breath of Homer, the charioteer of Plato, and — in Apuleius — the bride of Love who endures labours, fails, is rescued, and is enthroned on Olympus. Her name passed into every Western language as the word for mind itself.

cards.name: Soul
cards.desc: In Homer the psyche is the breath that leaves at death (Odyssey 11.488–491); in Plato it is the charioteer hitched to winged horses (Phaedrus 246a).

cards.name: Soul, breath
cards.desc: From ψύχω, 'to breathe, to blow' — the soul imagined as the cool breath that animates the body (Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek, s.v. ψυχή).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Psychḗ recovers the acute stress and long eta that plain ASCII psyche flattens.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in Greek as Ψυχή; immortalized by Apuleius's romance (Metamorphoses 4.28–6.24).

symbols.name: Butterfly
symbols.meaning: To the Greeks psyche was also the butterfly — the winged soul; Aristotle lists psyche among the insects (History of Animals 551a).

symbols.name: The lamp
symbols.meaning: The lamp Psyche raises over her sleeping husband — the test of trust that betrays love with a drop of hot oil.

symbols.name: West wind (Zephyr)
symbols.meaning: The wind that wafts her from the sacrificial crag to the hidden valley — nature itself escorting the soul.

symbols.name: Proserpina's box
symbols.meaning: The vessel of infernal beauty she is forbidden to open; curiosity releases sleep, not beauty.

symbols.name: Ant, reed, and eagle
symbols.meaning: The humble helpers of the four labours — smallness and patience succeeding where force fails.

mythology.lead: Psychḗ runs the whole arc of the Greek soul: in Homer she is the breath that leaves the dying; in Plato the immortal charioteer; in Apuleius the heroine who weds Love and is made a goddess. Her story — the only complete divine romance to survive from antiquity — became the West's standing parable of the soul's trials.

myths.title: The Breath That Leaves
myths.text:
In the earliest Greek, psyche is not a person but an event: the breath that leaves the body at death. When Odysseus meets the shade of Achilles in Hades and congratulates him on ruling the dead, the hero answers that he would rather live on earth as a landless serf than rule down here — and the word for that grieving shade is psyche (Homer, Odyssey 11.488–491). The Iliad sends Hector's psyche wailing down to Hades as his body is stripped on the plain (Iliad 22.362–363). There is no immortality yet, no judgment, no heaven — only a winged exhalation, faint and bloodless, craving offerings of blood in the dark.

The entire later career of the soul — as moral self, as divine spark — grows from this faint beginning: the breath, noticed at the moment it leaves.

myths.title: The Oracle of the Mountain
myths.text:
In Apuleius's romance a king with three daughters has a problem: the youngest, Psyche, is so beautiful that Venus's temples are abandoned for her, and no suitor dares approach. The oracle of Milesian Apollo gives a monstrous answer: expose the girl on a mountain crag to wed a dire, fierce, serpent-like evil (Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4.32–33). Left on the peak, Psyche is gathered up gently by the west wind, Zephyr, and set down in a flowered valley where a palace tends itself with bodiless voices. Her husband comes only in darkness and forbids the lamp: she must love what she cannot see, served by servants she cannot see, in a marriage she cannot inspect.

The trial begins the way every soul's trial begins — carried she knows not where, asked to trust what she cannot verify.

myths.title: The Drop of Hot Oil
myths.text:
Her jealous older sisters worm their way into the secret and convince her that her unseen husband is a coiling serpent who will devour her and her unborn child. Armed with lamp and razor she leans over the bed — and sees not a monster but the god of love himself, golden-winged, his bow and arrows set on the floor (Apuleius, Metamorphoses 5.7–23). In her shudder of joy a drop of hot oil leaps from the lamp and wakes him. He rises: love, he tells her, cannot live where trust does not dwell — and he is gone. Psyche wanders Greece searching, attempts the river in despair, and at last throws herself on Venus's mercy; the goddess, jealous and triumphant, sets her labours.

The myth's knife-edge: knowledge was within her reach, and it cost her everything — because it was taken, not given.

myths.title: Four Tasks and the Box of Beauty
myths.text:
Venus sets four impossible tasks. Sort a mountain heap of mixed grains by dawn — an ant takes pity and deploys its whole colony. Gather golden wool from the savage sheep of the riverbank — a speaking reed teaches her to wait and comb the fleece from the briars. Draw water from the Styx itself, gushing between cliffs — Jupiter's eagle stoops from the sky to fill her jug. Descend alive to the underworld and beg Proserpina for a box of her beauty — and the queen, compliant, fills it instead with a Stygian sleep. On the return, unable to resist, Psyche lifts the lid and is struck down on the road (Apuleius, Metamorphoses 6.10–21).

The soul's curriculum is humility: every task is accomplished by accepting help from below — ant, reed, eagle, and the queen of the dead herself.

myths.title: Wedded to Love on Olympus
myths.text:
Cupid, healed of his burn, finds her asleep on the earth and seals the infernal sleep back into the box. He flies to beg Jupiter, who overrules Venus and grants the girl immortality with a cup of ambrosia. The wedding is held on Olympus with the gods as guests, and from the marriage of Love and Soul is born a daughter named Voluptas — Greek Hēdonē, Pleasure (Apuleius, Metamorphoses 6.22–24). Later Platonists read the whole tale as allegory: the soul, fallen through its own curiosity, is lifted back by Love. And the folk-tale kin are vast — Apuleius's story is the earliest literary version of ATU 425, 'The Search for the Lost Husband,' the tale family that ends in Beauty and the Beast.

She alone of Greek heroines becomes a goddess not for bloodline or heroism but for surviving her own mistakes.

lore.syncretism: Later Platonism turned the romance into doctrine: for Plotinus and his successors Psyche's fall and ascent mirrored the soul's own, and Apuleius's tale — probably itself steeped in Mystery-lore — was read as an initiation text. Early Christian writers kept the image of the soul as bride but transferred the bridegroom to Christ; Origen's allegorical reading of the Song of Songs breathes the same air. In the Renaissance the pair became the favorite emblem of sacred and profane love together: Raphael's Loggia di Psiche (Villa Farnesina, 1518) and a flood of emblems, tapestries, and masques carried her through every European court. Neoplatonic allegory then hardened into science: where most goddesses faded, Psyche was reborn as Mind itself — the discipline of psychology took her name for its title.
lore.culturalLegacy: Psychḗ is one of the great donors to the world's vocabulary: psyche, psychic, psychology, psychiatry, psychedelic, psychosomatic — all borrow her name for the mind's phenomena. In art she had a second life unmatched by any Greek heroine: Roman frescoes, engraved gems, and sarcophagi of the butterfly-winged girl; Raphael's Farnesina loggia; Canova's Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss (1787–1793); Keats's 'Ode to Psyche' (1819), the first of his great odes, which apologizes for arriving late at her worship — she had, he said, no temple, choir, or oracle, so he would build them in verse. Every telling of Beauty and the Beast, every 'beastly husband' romance from Basile to Disney, descends from her night-lamp. The butterfly at the analyst's door and the honeymooner's myth are, equally, her shrines.
lore.extendedMeditation: Psychḗ is the rare figure whose name became the subject she personifies: the Greek word for breath ended up meaning the whole inner life, and then lent that meaning to a science. The myth tracks the deepening. Homer's psyche is barely a person — a wing of air leaving the mouth of the dying. Apuleius's Psyche is all too personal: jealous sisters, forbidden sight, a burned husband, labours assigned by a vindictive mother-in-law. Her ascent to Olympus is the ancient world's quietest theological statement: the soul is not born divine, it becomes divine — through error, service, humiliation, and a rescue it did not earn. Read allegorically, as the Neoplatonists did, the tale says the soul's worst enemy is curiosity severed from trust; read psychologically, as we cannot help doing, it says that love and mind are wedded or ruined together. That is why her name stands over the modern science of the mind: Psyche never ruled anything, yet everything inward answers to her.
lore.archaeology: No cult of Psyche is attested in the Greek world — she was worshipped in story before she was worshipped anywhere — but her image is common in Roman art: engraved gems and finger rings showing the butterfly-winged girl; frescoes of the tale's episodes; sarcophagus reliefs of Cupid and Psyche embracing, a favorite consolation image for the dead; and a Roman sculptural group of the winged pair in the Capitoline collections. The earliest certain reception is textual: within a century of Apuleius (c. 160s CE), the tale was famous across the empire. Her grandest shrines are later still — Raphael's Loggia di Psiche in Rome's Villa Farnesina (1517–1518) and Canova's Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss (1787–1793, Louvre and Hermitage). A goddess with no temple in antiquity built the finest ones of the Renaissance.
